summary: For ages 6-7: mentally find 10 more or 10 less than a two-digit number without counting on in ones, by recognising that adding/subtracting a ten changes only the tens digit while the ones digit stays the same (10 more than 56 is 66; 10 less is 46). The core objective is reasoning plus fluency: the child should both produce the answer instantly and explain why only the tens digit changes. Concrete models (100-square vertical moves, base-ten rods) build the insight; timed recall practice consolidates it once understanding is secure. Keep examples within the two-digit range where only the tens digit changes by one.
misconceptions: Counting on in ones (56, 57, 58…66) instead of jumping a ten — no place-value shortcut.
Changing the ones digit as well, or changing the wrong digit (56 → 57 for '10 more').
Miscounting on the 100-square by moving diagonally or the wrong direction.
Struggling at decade boundaries because the pattern is memorised without understanding the tens digit's role.

activities.title: The 100-square vertical jump
steps: Point to a starting number on a 100-square (for example 56).

On a 100-square numbered from the top (1-10 in the top row), to find 10 more, move straight DOWN exactly one row, staying in the same column; to find 10 less, move straight UP one row in the same column. (On a bottom-up 100-square the directions are reversed. Check which way the numbers grow on your grid.)
Say the new number aloud (56 → 66 for 10 more, 56 → 46 for 10 less).
Repeat the +10 jump several times to trace a straight vertical stripe down the grid: 56 → 66 → 76 → 86.
Each time, name the ones digit and the tens digit and state what changed: 'the ones stayed 6, the tens went up by one.'
activities.insight: Adding or subtracting ten is always the same move — straight down or up one row — and the ones digit never moves because only a whole ten is added or removed.

activities.title: Add or remove one ten-rod
steps: Lay out a two-digit number with base-ten tens-rods and ones-cubes (for example 5 rods and 6 cubes for 56).
To add 10, place exactly ONE more rod; to subtract 10, take exactly ONE rod away.
Watch the ones-cubes the whole time and say aloud that they did not move.
Read the new total and state which digit changed (the tens) and which stayed the same (the ones).
activities.insight: Adding ten means adding a single ten-rod, which changes the tens count by one and leaves the ones completely untouched.

activities.title: Ten more versus one more
steps: For the same starting number (for example 56), find 1 more and then 10 more; then find 1 less and 10 less.
Say which digit changes each time: 1 more changes the ones (56 → 57); 10 more changes the tens (56 → 66).
Explain in your own words how '10 more' is different from '1 more.'
activities.insight: Changing the ones digit (±1) and changing the tens digit (±10) are distinct moves; the child must adjust the correct digit for the correct operation.

activities.title: Mental fluency and explanation
steps: Answer rapid spoken or written items: 10 more than 73? (83) 10 less than 40? (30) 10 more than 56? (66) 10 less than 56? (46).
Give each answer without fingers or counting on in ones.
Complete a +10 chain by filling blanks: 46 → 56 → 66 → __ (76).
After answering, state which digit changed and why the ones digit did not.
Rehearse items that cross a decade boundary while the result stays a two-digit number (for example 10 more than 85 is 95, 10 less than 40 is 30) to check the pattern holds.
activities.insight: Once the place-value reason is understood, 10 more/10 less becomes instant recall produced by a single tens-digit change rather than by counting, for results that remain two-digit numbers.

checkQuestion: Ask quickly and watch how they get the answer (fingers? counting? or instant?): '10 more than 56? ... 10 less than 56? ... 10 more than 73? ... 10 less than 40?' Watch whether the tens digit jumps in one move.
checkAnswer: 66, 46, 83, 30 — produced instantly by changing the tens digit by one, without counting on in ones.
